blocks.text: Every tool call and every piece of context an AI model ever uses through MCP ultimately comes from somewhere, and that somewhere is a server. A server is the role that does the actual work: wrapping a real system, exposing what it can do in a standard shape, and answering whatever any connected client asks of it. This lesson goes deep on what makes a good MCP server, and why the same server can be reused, unmodified, by completely different hosts.
1. What a Server Actually Is

blocks.alt: An existing system goes through a server to become an MCP capability
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738492-633809498.png

An MCP server is a program that exposes a set of capabilities, tools to invoke, resources to read, and prompts to select, over the MCP protocol, so that any connected client can discover and use them. It does not embed an AI model, it does not decide what to do with results, and it has no idea what host or application is ultimately behind the client talking to it.

In the simplest terms, a server answers questions and does things when asked, nothing more. If a client sends a well formed request the server understands, it acts and replies. It never initiates a conversation with a model, and it never reaches out to a host uninvited, all communication is client initiated.

A simple way to spot a server in the wild: it is the thing that only ever responds, it never starts a conversation on its own initiative. If a component in your system reaches out unprompted to begin something, it is playing the host or client role, not the server role.
2. Wrapping an Existing System or API

Servers are rarely built from nothing. Almost every real MCP server exists to wrap something that already exists: a database, an internal REST API, a file system, a ticketing system, a piece of internal company infrastructure that predates MCP entirely. The server job is to translate that existing systems capabilities into the standard shapes MCP expects.

This wrapping role is exactly what makes MCP valuable at scale. A company with an internal ticketing API does not need to teach every single AI application how that API works, it writes one server that wraps the API once, and every MCP compatible host can use it from that point on, without ever learning the underlying APIs specific quirks.

blocks.title: Servers rarely invent new capability
blocks.content: The overwhelming majority of useful MCP servers do not invent brand new functionality, they expose functionality that already existed somewhere, a database, an API, a file system, in the standard shape MCP expects. Building a server is usually a translation exercise more than a from scratch engineering exercise.

blocks.text: 3. Exposing Tools, Resources, and Prompts

blocks.alt: A server exposes tools, resources, and prompts
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738494-306284434.png

A server communicates what it can do through three primitives. Tools are actions the model can invoke, with side effects. Resources are readable pieces of context, like files or records, with no side effects. Prompts are reusable instruction templates a user or client can select. Each of these gets its own dedicated lesson right after this one, but it is worth seeing all three side by side here.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Primitive","What it represents","Does it have side effects"],"rows":[["Tool","An action the model can invoke","Often yes"],["Resource","A readable piece of context","No, read only"],["Prompt","A reusable instruction template","No, it just shapes a conversation"]]}

blocks.text: A server is not required to expose all three. Plenty of real servers expose only tools, or only resources, depending on what the underlying system they wrap actually needs to offer.
4. Statelessness: Why Servers Do Not Remember Clients

blocks.alt: A server has no memory of individual clients
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738494-912263277.png

A well designed MCP server treats each incoming request largely on its own terms, rather than depending on a long private memory of everything a particular client has said before. Session level bookkeeping, like the negotiated protocol version, is fine to hold onto for the life of a connection, but business logic state, like a half finished multi step transaction, should not silently live only in server memory tied to one specific connection.

This matters because it keeps a server simple to reason about, easy to restart, and easy to scale by running several instances behind a load balancer if needed. A server that secretly depends on remembering exactly which client asked what earlier becomes fragile the moment a connection drops and reconnects, or the moment two instances of the server run side by side.

blocks.title: What state is fine to keep
blocks.content: Protocol level session state, like which capabilities were negotiated during the handshake, is expected and normal to hold per connection. What should be avoided is business state that only exists in server memory and would be lost or duplicated the moment the process restarts or scales out.

blocks.text: One practical test for statelessness: could you kill the server process and immediately start a fresh one, with a new client reconnecting from scratch, and have it behave identically to how the original process would have behaved for that same request. If the answer is no because some important state only ever lived in the now dead process, that is a sign business logic state leaked somewhere it should not have.
5. Reusable Across Many Different Hosts

Because a server has no idea what host is behind the client talking to it, and makes no assumptions about how its results will be used, the exact same server binary can be connected to a chat assistant, a coding tool, and an autonomous agent framework, all at once or at different times, with zero changes to the server itself.

This reusability is the direct payoff of keeping servers narrow and stateless. A team that builds one solid file system server can publish it once, and every host in the ecosystem that wants file system access can connect to that exact same server, rather than every host team writing and maintaining their own separate integration with the file system.
6. A Server Can Serve Many Clients at Once

blocks.alt: A server serves client 1 and client 2 at once
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738495-378815267.png

While each client only ever talks to one server, the reverse is not true: a single running server can have many separate client connections open to it at the same time, from different hosts, or even from several instances of the same host. Every one of those connections gets its own independent session on the server side.

This is a natural consequence of statelessness. A server that does not lean on fragile per client memory for anything beyond protocol bookkeeping has no trouble handling many simultaneous, independent conversations, the same way a well built web server handles many simultaneous requests without them interfering with each other.

This is also why a server should never assume anything about ordering across different client connections. Two clients calling the same tool moments apart are entirely independent events from the servers point of view, and a correct server implementation never lets one client connections in flight request affect how it responds to a different client connections request.
7. Declaring Capabilities During Initialization

When a client connects, the very first thing a server does is participate in the initialize handshake, where it declares which capability categories it supports, tools, resources, prompts, and any optional features like sending log messages or notifying about list changes. This declaration happens once, right at the start of a session, covered in full depth in a dedicated later lesson.
8. The Server Side of Discovery: List Operations

After the handshake, a client typically asks the server to list what it actually offers. On the server side, this means responding to methods like tools/list, resources/list, and prompts/list with the concrete, current menu of what is available, including each items name, description, and schema.

A server that later adds or removes something from one of these lists, say a new tool becomes available after a feature flag is turned on, should send a corresponding list changed notification so connected clients know to refresh their cached view rather than working off a stale list.

items: tools/list, returning every currently available tool, its description, and its input schema
resources/list, returning every currently available resource and the URI that identifies it
prompts/list, returning every currently available prompt template and its parameters

blocks.text: 9. Executing a Tool Call: What Happens Server Side

blocks.alt: A tool call request executes on the server to produce a result
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738495-390158286.png

When a tools/call request arrives, the server validates the arguments against the schema it originally advertised, executes whatever real world action the tool represents, and returns a result, or a structured error if something went wrong. This is usually the most consequential moment in the whole request lifecycle, since it is where an actual side effect against a real system happens.
9.1 Validation Before Execution

A careful server implementation never trusts incoming arguments blindly, even though the client presumably already validated them against the advertised schema on its side. Revalidating on the server protects against a client bug, a stale cached schema, or, in less trusted environments, a deliberately malformed request.
10. Local Servers vs Remote Servers

blocks.alt: A local server is compared against a remote server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738496-887575731.png

Some servers run as a local subprocess launched directly by the host, communicating over standard input and output, ideal for wrapping something local like a file system. Others run as a standing remote service reachable over a network based transport, ideal for wrapping a shared resource many different users need to reach, like a company wide database.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Deployment style","Typical transport","Good fit for"],"rows":[["Local subprocess","Standard input and output","Local file access, local developer tools"],["Remote service","Network based, often HTTP based","Shared company systems, services many users need access to"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Server Authentication and Authorization

A remote server in particular usually needs to know who is calling it, both to authenticate the connecting client and to authorize which specific actions that caller is allowed to take. This typically layers standard mechanisms, like tokens or API keys, underneath the MCP protocol itself, since MCP does not reinvent authentication from scratch.

A local subprocess server often skips heavy authentication, since simply being launched by the host as a trusted child process is itself a reasonable proof of legitimacy, though it should still enforce authorization for what any given operation is allowed to touch, especially for anything filesystem or credential related.

Authorization at the server level often needs to be finer grained than a simple yes or no on connecting at all. A single authenticated client might be allowed to call some tools but not others, or read some resources but not others, and a well built server enforces that finer grained check on every individual request, not only once at connection time.
12. Server Implementations in Practice

Just like with clients, you rarely hand roll the protocol plumbing for a server from scratch. The official SDKs provide decorators or registration functions that let you write a plain function, mark it as a tool, resource, or prompt, and have the SDK handle schema generation, request routing, and response formatting for you.
13. Designing a Good Server: Small, Focused, Well Described

The best MCP servers tend to be narrow and focused, wrapping one coherent system well, rather than trying to be an everything server bolting together unrelated capabilities. A file system server that also happens to send emails is a sign of scope creep that makes the server harder to reason about, harder to secure, and harder to reuse cleanly.

items: Give every tool a clear, specific name and an honest, complete description of what it does
Keep a server focused on one coherent system or domain rather than bundling unrelated capabilities together
Design input schemas that reject bad input clearly rather than silently accepting near misses
Avoid leaning on hidden server side memory that a client has no way of knowing about

blocks.text: A useful sanity check when designing a new server is to describe it in one sentence to a colleague who has never seen it. If that sentence needs the word "and" more than once to cover everything it does, that is often a sign the server is trying to be more than one focused thing at once.
14. Server Failure and Error Reporting

When something goes wrong inside a server, whether the underlying system it wraps is down or the request itself was invalid, the server has a responsibility to report that failure back as a clear, structured error rather than crashing the whole process or returning a misleadingly successful looking response.

A server crash takes down every connected client at once, which is disproportionate for what might be a single bad request. Robust servers isolate failures per request wherever possible, catching exceptions around individual tool executions so a fault in one call does not bring down the whole server process and every other in flight session with it.
15. Server vs a Traditional Backend API

blocks.alt: An MCP server is compared against a traditional backend API
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738496-399397838.png

It is fair to ask what actually distinguishes an MCP server from a traditional backend API, since both often wrap the same underlying systems. The difference is not in what work gets done, it is in the discovery and description layer: an MCP server describes itself, its tools, its input schemas, in a standard, machine readable way that any MCP client can understand without prior documentation reading.

A traditional API instead usually requires a human developer to read documentation and hand write integration code for every single consuming application. An MCP server removes that hand written integration step for every AI application that speaks MCP, which is the entire point of the standard in the first place.
16. Versioning a Server Over Time

A server is rarely finished the day it ships. Tools get added, input schemas get refined, bugs get fixed. Because clients discover a servers capabilities live at connection time rather than relying on a fixed contract baked in at build time, a server can evolve fairly freely as long as it keeps sending list changed notifications when something meaningful shifts.

The one thing a server should avoid is silently changing the meaning of an existing tool name, for instance narrowing what arguments it accepts, without any signal at all. A client that cached the old schema, or a model that learned the old behavior from an earlier turn, can be caught off guard. Safer evolutions add a new tool alongside the old one, or bump a reported server version so callers can notice something changed.

blocks.text: 17. When Multiple Servers Overlap in Capability

It is entirely possible for two independently built servers to offer similar or even overlapping capabilities, two different teams might each publish a web search server, for instance. MCP does not prevent this, and it does not pick a winner, a host that connects to both simply sees two separate tools and, along with the model, decides which one to use.

This overlap is usually harmless and sometimes healthy, since it lets a host or user choose the implementation they trust most. Problems only arise if a host fails to disambiguate identically named tools clearly, which is why that responsibility was called out specifically in the host lesson as something the host, not the server, must handle.
Worked Example

A team wraps their internal customer database as an MCP server, exposing one tool, look_up_customer, and one resource type, customer records identified by a URI. The server declares tools and resources capability during handshake, then any connected host, a support assistant, an internal ops chatbot, an autonomous billing agent, can all reuse the exact same server.

Neither the support assistant host nor the billing agent host had to write any database specific code themselves. Both simply connect to this one server and immediately get the same look_up_customer tool and the same customer resource, exactly the reuse MCP is designed to unlock.
Common Mistakes

items: Baking business logic state into server memory tied to one specific client connection, making the server fragile to restarts and hard to scale.
Building an everything server that bundles unrelated capabilities together instead of staying focused on one coherent system.
Trusting client side validation and skipping server side validation of tool arguments entirely.
Letting one failed request crash the whole server process, taking down every other connected client along with it.
Forgetting to send a list changed notification after tools, resources, or prompts change, leaving clients working off stale cached data.
Writing vague tool descriptions that leave a model guessing about what a tool actually does or expects.

blocks.text: Many of these mistakes share a common root cause: designing a server around what is convenient for todays one caller rather than around what will remain correct and safe once several different, unrelated hosts start relying on it at once.
Practice

Design a small MCP server wrapping a fictional internal inventory system. Expose one tool, check_stock, that takes a product id and returns the quantity on hand, with proper server side validation and a clear error if the product id does not exist. Then write the resource definition for reading a single product record by id.

code.content:
@server.tool()
async def check_stock(product_id: str) -> dict:
    # TODO: validate product_id is well formed before querying
    # TODO: look up the product; raise a clear error if not found
    # TODO: return the quantity on hand
    pass

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A server exposes tools, resources, and prompts by wrapping some real underlying system, staying stateless and narrowly focused so it can be reused unmodified across many different hosts and serve many client connections at once. It never embeds a model, never decides what to do with its own results, and never assumes anything about who is ultimately behind the client calling it.

With host, client, and server all covered as roles, the next lesson zooms into the first of the three server side primitives in real depth, tools, the actions a model can invoke, including their schemas, their side effects, and how a server describes them well enough for a model to use them correctly.
